pages.summary: Morphology: images grown, shrunk, opened and closed by a structuring element.
body: A structuring element is a flat neighbourhood: a disk, square, rectangle, diamond, line or octagon, or any logical matrix (`SE.Neighborhood`). Dilation takes the largest value under it at each pixel, erosion the smallest; opening (erosion then dilation) takes away bright details smaller than the element, closing (dilation then erosion) fills dark gaps smaller than it. The top-hats give what opening took away (`imtophat`) and what closing filled (`imbothat`), which picks out small bright or dark details on an uneven background. Logical images give logical images.

examples.title: Specks and gaps

pages.summary: Holes filled, reconstruction from markers, and objects at the border taken away.
body: `imfill(BW, 'holes')` fills the background that cannot be reached from the image's edge; with locations, it floods the background from those points. `imreconstruct` dilates a marker repeatedly while keeping it under a mask, until it stops changing: for binary images, the objects of the mask that the marker touches. `imclearborder` takes away the objects (or for gray images the light structures) connected to the border.

examples.title: Rings filled, an object picked, the border cleared

pages.summary: Regional extremes of an image, the shallow ones suppressed, and minima imposed.
body: A regional maximum is a plateau whose neighbours all lie lower (8-connected); `imregionalmax` and `imregionalmin` mark them. `imhmax` takes down every maximum by h (the reconstruction of I - h under I), so that maxima less than h high vanish; `imhmin` fills minima less than h deep. `imextendedmax` and `imextendedmin` are the regional extremes that survive that. `imimposemin` changes an image so that its only regional minima are where a mask says, the usual step before `watershed`.
syntax: Maxima lower than H taken down.

examples.title: Two peaks and a ripple

pages.summary: The watershed transform: an image's catchment basins, with ridges between them.
body: The image is seen as a landscape flooded from its regional minima (Meyer's method): each pixel joins the basin it fills from, labelled 1, 2, ... (by their minima's first pixels down the columns), and where basins meet a ridge of 0 is left. To split touching objects, flood the negative of their distance transform; to avoid one basin per noise dip, impose the minima first.

examples.title: Two touching discs split

pages.summary: The objects of a binary image: found, numbered and measured.
body: `bwlabel` numbers the 8-connected components (4 if asked) in the order their first pixel comes down the columns; `bwlabeln` does it in any number of dimensions. `bwconncomp` gives them as a struct of linear indices. `regionprops` measures each region (of a binary image, a label matrix or `bwconncomp`'s struct): Area, Centroid and BoundingBox by default, and many more by name, also with an intensity image; `'table'` gives a table.
syntax: As a table, with an intensity image.

examples.title: Three objects measured

pages.summary: Binary shapes thinned, outlined and traced.
body: `bwmorph` applies an operation n times (Inf: until nothing changes): 'skel', 'thin', 'shrink', 'remove', 'spur', 'endpoints', 'branchpoints', 'clean', 'fill', 'majority' and more. `bwskel` thins objects to lines one pixel wide, pruning branches shorter than `'MinBranchLength'`. `bwperim` keeps the pixels with an off neighbour. `bwboundaries` gives each object's boundary (and each hole's) as rows of [row col], clockwise and closed; `bwtraceboundary` traces one from a pixel on it.

examples.title: A plus sign's skeleton and outline

pages.summary: Objects kept or removed by their area, a property, or a pixel.
body: `bwareaopen` removes objects of fewer than P pixels; `bwareafilt` keeps those with an area within a range, or the n largest or smallest; `bwpropfilt` does the same by any regionprops property with one value per object; `bwselect` keeps the objects that hold given pixels (column, row).

examples.title: Objects of several sizes

pages.summary: Distances to objects, convex hulls, Euler numbers and areas.
body: `bwdist` gives each pixel's distance to the nearest on pixel (Euclidean, city-block, chessboard or quasi-Euclidean), as single, and that pixel's index. `bwconvhull` gives the convex hull of all the on pixels, or of each object. `bweuler` counts objects less holes. `bwarea` estimates the area by weighting each 2-by-2 pattern, closer to a continuous shape's area than counting pixels.

examples.title: A ring, a dot and an L
